The history of measuring time runs from shadows to atoms. Early sundials divided daylight into parts by the length and angle of a shadow, which worked only when the sun was out and drifted with the seasons. Water clocks let a vessel fill or drain at a steady rate, so they could keep going at night and indoors, and some carried floats that moved pointers or struck bells. Mechanical clocks appeared in European towers in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. They were driven by falling weights and regulated by an escapement, a device that lets the gear train advance in small, regular steps. The verge and foliot escapement was crude, and those early clocks could gain or lose a quarter of an hour in a day, which is why many had no minute hand at all. The pendulum changed that. Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656, and because a pendulum's swing takes nearly the same time whatever its width, the error fell to around a minute a day and later to seconds. The anchor escapement and the temperature-compensated pendulum improved it further, and by the nineteenth century observatories kept regulator clocks that could hold a fraction of a second over weeks. At sea the problem was harder, since a pendulum is useless on a rolling ship, and finding longitude depends on knowing the time at a reference meridian. John Harrison's marine chronometers solved it in the eighteenth century with springs, balances and materials chosen to cancel the effects of heat and cold. Quartz crystal oscillators arrived in the twentieth century. A piece of quartz cut the right way vibrates at a precise frequency when a voltage is applied, and counting those vibrations gives a timebase far steadier than any pendulum. Atomic clocks went further again. They lock an oscillator to the frequency of a transition between energy levels of an atom, usually caesium or rubidium, and since 1967 the second has been defined as a fixed number of periods of the radiation from a caesium transition. Optical clocks, which use transitions at much higher frequencies, are now so stable that they would drift by less than a second over the age of the universe, and they can detect the slowing of time caused by raising them a few centimetres in Earth's gravity. Each step made the ticking smaller and steadier, and each changed what people could build: railways needed standard time, navigation needed chronometers, and satellite positioning needs clocks good to a few billionths of a second.
